title: What Worked Examples Work Best?
author: Dominic Salles
summary: Salles describes rebuilding his exam guides around dozens of marked student answers instead of teacher exposition, and asks whether teaching only from grade 9 essays is the best use of worked examples. He argues that literature is about knowing more ideas and evidence rather than grasping harder concepts, so top essays hand weaker students that knowledge directly. He is torn on whether to show grade 7 and 9 side by side. A recent study found that students studying top-grade examples graded their own work better, but he criticises it for asking the less useful question and probably confirming the researchers' hypothesis. The piece ends with a self-imposed test: try to disprove his own assumption through a money-back course.
points: Teaching from several top-grade essays, including ones that contradict each other, is less reductive than it sounds and invites students to debate and synthesise.
Moving up the grades in literature is mostly a matter of knowing more evidence and weighing more ideas, so essays can transfer that knowledge directly.
The cited study measured self-assessment accuracy rather than writing performance, which is the more useful question.
Confirmation bias afflicts teachers and researchers alike, so Salles advocates designing tests that try to falsify what you believe.
quotes: I might teach one essay that suggests Scrooge is a two dimensional cypher, whose redemption is unrealistic and plot device rather than convincing portray. Then a second might argue that Scrooge’s redemption is deeply rooted in psychological truth, with specific regard to attachment theory.
Students could then produce their own oral and written responses where they debate and synthesise such views, establishing a voice and argument of their own.
This found that university students who studied top grade worked examples were better at grading their own work than students who studied low grade examples.

Literature is not like maths - to move up the grades students don’t have to understand conceptually more difficult ideas. They simply have to weigh up the merits of more ideas. In other words, they simply have to know a lot more.
Unfortunately, as so often with research, the researchers tried to answer the less useful question, because they probably looked for results to confirm their hypothesis.
Whereas my approach is the opposite - set up an experiment to test whether my assumptions are false.
